pass_a_gloss: [...] [Lemma, Isaiah 36:4-6:] And Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the king, the great king of Assyrians: Is a battle line made in counsel or in words of lips? And now upon whom have you trusted, that you disobey me? Behold, you are trusting upon the reed staff, this broken one, upon Egypt; whoever leans upon it, it will enter into his hand. This is Pharaoh king of Egypt, and all those who trust upon him. The gates clearly having been shut, and the people, surely the most warlike, standing upon the walls, there went out to Rabshakeh, fulfilling the need of the embassies, the chosen [men] of the king and those foremost among the priests. But he, being of Persian cruelty, and having a mouth speaking great things, according to what is written, grew bold against the glory of God. And he names Hezekiah by bare calling, not having added king, nor any other of all the things most fitting to those in such pre-eminences. But the king of the Assyrians he does not call simply this very thing, but also calls him great. And he says that, Is a battle line made in counsel or in words of lips? For since the Jews, having the law through Moses, were thought wiser than the other nations; and indeed they were saying: Blessed are we, Israel, because the things pleasing to the Lord are known to us; Rabshakeh brings down to nothing the boast upon this, saying that, war and battle being at hand, there will be wholly useless for help to them both the [skill] in knowing of laws, and the shrewdness in counsels alone, and the very practisedness, as it were, in words. And since some of those who had reigned over Judaea had called the hand of the Egyptians to help, although doing this outlandishly, the Assyrian thought now too that Hezekiah trusted not rather upon God, but upon some others, rather upon those holding the land of the Egyptians. For this reason he names it a reed staff. For rotten somehow, he says, and easily broken always, is the hope upon those, and wronging rather than being able to profit those who use it; just as indeed also a reed staff, on which if someone rests, he will wholly shatter it, and it will wrong the one who trusted upon it. [Lemma, Isaiah 36:7-9:] But if you say: Upon the Lord our God we have trusted, now mix with my lord the king of Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horse, if you will be able to give riders upon them. And how can you turn back to the face of one governor? He is loose-mouthed again, and lifts the horn into height, and speaks injustice against God. For if indeed, he says, you have trusted upon him, mix with my lord, that is, arm yourselves fully and stand for battle. And I will add also two thousand horses for you, and this will suffice [the section breaks off].
pass_b_english: … “And Rabshakeh said to them: Say to Hezekiah, Thus says the king, the great king of the Assyrians: Is a battle line drawn up by counsel, or by words of the lips? And now, in whom have you put your trust, that you disobey me? Behold, you have put your trust in this staff of reed, this broken staff, in Egypt; whoever leans on it, it will go into his hand. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt, and all who trust in him” (Isaiah 36:4-6).

The gates, clearly, had been shut, and the people, no doubt the most warlike of them, stood on the walls; and to carry out the business of the embassy, the king's chosen men and the foremost among the priests went out to Rabshakeh. But he, a man of Persian savagery, with “a mouth speaking great things,” as it is written (Daniel 7:8), grew insolent against the glory of God. He calls Hezekiah by his bare name, without adding “king” or any other of the titles that best befit men in such high stations. But the king of the Assyrians he does not simply call by that title; he calls him great as well.

And he says: “Is a battle line drawn up by counsel, or by words of the lips?” For the Jews, who had the Law given through Moses, were thought wiser than the other nations; indeed, they used to say, “Blessed are we, Israel, because what is pleasing to the Lord is known to us” (Baruch 4:4). So Rabshakeh brings their boast in this to nothing, saying that when war and battle are upon them, all this will be wholly useless to help them: their knowledge of the laws, their shrewdness in counsels alone, and even their practised skill, as it were, in words.

And since some of those who had reigned over Judea had called on the hand of the Egyptians for help, though in doing so they acted most wrongly, the Assyrian supposed that now too Hezekiah was trusting not in God but in others, or rather in those who held the land of the Egyptians. That is why he calls it a staff of reed. For the hope placed in them, he says, is rotten and always easily broken, and it harms those who rely on it rather than being able to help them, just like a staff of reed: if anyone leans his weight on it, he will surely break it, and it will hurt the man who trusted in it.

“But if you say, We have put our trust in the Lord our God, now engage my lord the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able to provide riders for them. And how can you turn back the face of a single governor?” (Isaiah 36:7-9).

He runs loose at the mouth again, lifts his horn on high, and speaks injustice against God (Psalm 75:5). For if indeed, he says, you have put your trust in Him, engage my lord, that is, arm yourselves and stand ready for battle. And I will add two thousand horses for you, and this will be enough …

choices.why: Rabshakeh withholds Hezekiah's royal title while calling his own king great.
ἐντριβής, well practised; Rabshakeh mocks skill in words as useless in war.
μίγνυμι of meeting in battle; Cyril glosses it 'arm yourselves and stand ready for battle'.

choices.english: He runs loose at the mouth
choices.why: ἀθυροστομέω, to have a mouth without a door.
The hope placed in Egypt is like a rotten reed.
